extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers studying Henry James, fiction theory, or literary criticism
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of The Art of Fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Background and interpretive notes on Henry James's essay "The Art of Fiction," summarizing his aesthetic principles for the novel (what fiction should do and how it should be written). Useful for students preparing literary analysis or contextualizing James's influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interestingness as the novel's primary requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: "The novel ... must satisfy only one requirement: to be interesting."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: James explicitly states that the novel's chief obligation is to interest the reader; this is presented as the sole necessary requirement for fiction, implying that artistic success is measured first by the capacity to engage attention rather than by adherence to external moral aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of didactic/moral purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: James responds to Sir Walter Besant's claim that the main purpose of literature is to carry a moral criterion and disagrees with that position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critic/author should avoid treating fiction primarily as a vehicle for moral instruction; instead, James argues for a different end (impressionistic representation of life). This functions as an evaluative standard against overly moralizing or preachy works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novel as an impression of life (imprint on the mind)
rubrics_metrics.description: James claims that a novel is an impression of life, "which in turn is an imprint left on one’s mind."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction should aim to produce an enduring psychological or perceptual impression on the reader rather than merely recording events. Evaluate works by the vividness and persistence of their impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize representing impressions over reporting events
rubrics_metrics.description: James preferred describing not an event, but someone's impression of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narration should foreground characters' perceptions and responses; scenes and actions are valuable insofar as they convey subjective experience. Avoid evaluating fiction solely on plot-event reporting when it neglects interior perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimentation with form and new narrative methods
rubrics_metrics.description: James was one of the first writers to consciously experiment with the literary form. He sought to see and portray life in a new way, using new methods of narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovative narrative techniques and formal experimentation (e.g., shifts in point of view, indirect presentation of consciousness) are endorsed as valid and valuable means to achieve deeper impressions of life; evaluation should credit formal risk and originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatization of consciousness / subjective writing (precursor to stream of consciousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique he developed for dramatizing the hero’s thoughts left a deep mark in the history of literature and stood at the origins of modernist techniques of subjective writing which later developed into the 'stream of consciousness' technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective fiction often dramatizes inner thought processes rather than summarizing them; techniques that render subjective experience (interior monologue, shifting focalization) are central to James's standard and to later modernist practice.
